items.content:
The Founding Fathers understood that declaring independence wasn't just about civil liberties. It was also about trade - and, yes, supply chains.
🇺🇸 https://lnkd.in/eAnMPWXb

America would not last long if it could not also be commercially vibrant on the world stage.

Among the "facts" used to justify the Declaration of Independence, we find: 
“For cutting off our Trade with all parts of the world”

Beyond the desire to be self-governed, global supply chains played a critical role in the American Colonies’ decision to break away from Great Britain. This gives modern supply chain professionals a direct connection to our Colonial predecessors.

As we mark the 250-year anniversary of the Declaration of Independence (and celebrate that we've patched things up with the English!! 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 ), it is fascinating to remember the commercial and trade-based ties we share with those who went before us.

Happy Birthday, America!

#supplychain #4thofJuly #America250

items.content:
AIS - the Automatic Identification System that ships use to broadcast information about their identity, location, and destination - was first envisioned in the 1960s by Swedish seaman Benny Pettersson.

Today, it is an essential part of maritime safety... but it is under attack.

AIS is based on the premise of mutual benefit. That vessels can operate more safely when they know who is around them and where they are going.

The stakes are higher than ever in the Strait of Hormuz, and it is taking a toll on AIS. Ships are spoofing, trolling, turning off their AIS signals, and using them as a means of communication. 

We're watching as trust in the system slowly but surely erodes...

In this week's Art of Supply, I share the history of AIS, how it is supposed to work, and why it became so successful, and speculate about whether it will survive the current challenges.

items.content:
Supplier innovation is a shared responsibility.

Can you imagine being the person at The Coca-Cola Company that manages the McDonald's account? It must be like having two heavyweight bosses.

McDonald’s has reportedly been pushing Coke to innovate, asking for drinks that will help drive sales like the ones offered at Dunkin'​ and Starbucks. 

Several tests (like a machine that lets you make your own drink blend, and Vitaminwater) missed the mark. 

Now McDonald's has rolled out a new line of custom-crafted sodas, including the trendy “dirty soda” concept, which mixes traditional sodas with syrup or cream.

In advertising posters, they are indeed “TikTok-ready” as described by The Wall Street Journal.

But… that all depends on local McDonald's execution. 

I am not a regular soda drinker, but even I was curious about the dirty soda trend (marketing objective achieved). I bought a Sprite Berry Blast - a beautiful blue soda with cold white foam on top. 

When I got it, it was in a standard, non-translucent paper cup, and through the lid, it looked green. I assumed it was the wrong drink. Honestly, I thought it was a Shamrock Shake. 

The McDonald's employee explained that the cup lid was green. Total miss!

One way to see this story is that Coke is falling short on beverage innovation, but if the two companies want this 70-year partnership to last, they need to collaborate on execution as well as product development and marketing.

Supplier co-innovation sounds great - and it IS great - when done well. 

At the same time, what is required for success may be more than either side expects. In some cases, the best thing they can do is share the responsibility for successes and failures.

Read more here: https://lnkd.in/e-sAC6c4

The Bayeux Tapestry is a 950-year-old embroidery that depicts the events leading to the Battle of Hastings in 1066, when William the Conqueror took control of England (and King Harold was famously shot in the eye by an arrow).

That something has survived so long and offers so much detail is remarkable. 

The tapestry is about to travel to England on loan from France. What kind of logistics are needed to move something so delicate and precious?

As detailed in the BBC article below, in a specially-made crate, in a cage, on a truck, under the English Channel, and in secrecy. They have done two test runs, and the shock-absorbing provisions reportedly reduce the impact on the tapestry to no more than what is caused by tourists in a museum gallery.

Read more here: https://lnkd.in/e37kw-Ba

If you're interested in learning more about the Bayeux Tapestry, I highly recommend the Curiosity Stream (Curiosity Inc.) documentary about it.

items.content:
"No, no, no -- I can't do that!" This was what the American NUMMI leaders said to Isao Yoshino when they came to Japan and were asked to "pull the #andon" or stop the line.

At the GM plant where they had worked previously, they would have been yelled at or fired for signalling a problem. 

And they certainly wouldn't have been responded to with help.

At Toyota they were being asked to signal every problem. Every challenge. It's every person's job to ensure quality on the line and not to pass on problems.

And to their surprise, they were rewarded with support.

It's not the signal that is most important. It's leaders' response. 

Andon is what changed their minds.

And Isao Yoshino believes it is what ultimately changed the NUMMI culture and created one of the most famous business turnarounds ever, going from the worst performing GE plant to the best in less than one year. 

Tune in to hear (or watch) Mr. Yoshino talk about the power of #andon and "Bad News First" in this special episode of Chain of Learning.

In my latest IndustryWeek article, I share stories from these three companies and how their leaders including Larry Culp (of GE) think about their role in welcoming and responding to bad news and problems.

"No, no, no -- I can't do that!" This was what the American NUMMI leaders said to Isao Yoshino when they came to Japan and were asked to "pull the #andon" or stop the line.

At the GM plant where they had worked previously, they would have been yelled at or fired for signalling a problem. 

And they certainly wouldn't have been responded to with help.

At Toyota they were being asked to signal every problem. Every challenge. It's every person's job to ensure quality on the line and not to pass on problems.

And to their surprise, they were rewarded with support.

It's not the signal that is most important. It's leaders' response. 

Andon is what changed their minds.

And Isao Yoshino believes it is what ultimately changed the NUMMI culture and created one of the most famous business turnarounds ever, going from the worst performing GE plant to the best in less than one year. 

Tune in to hear (or watch) Mr. Yoshino talk about the power of #andon and "Bad News First" in this special episode of Chain of Learning.

I had no idea if my interview ever aired, until Mr. Yoshino emailed me last night to say he'd spotted me on the clip. He wasn't expecting to see me either. :)

🎥 The link to watch my short clip is in the comments 👇

In May 2025, I'd just landed in Japan to host my Japan Leadership Experience, with plans to spend a few days in my former home city of Tokyo before traveling to Nagoya to kick off the program.

Moments after clearing customs and immigration at Haneda, I followed my usual process of heading to Yamato Transport's desk to ship my larger luggage ahead to Nagoya so I didn't have to lug it with me on the trains.

A reporter stopped me to ask what I think about Yamato Transport.

It's more than a luggage delivery service where you can ship your luggage (or skis, or anything!) from one destination to the next, easily and quickly. 

It's one of the Japanese services that I LOVE and miss the most when I'm not in the country. It's SO easy, convenient, cheap, and reliable.

What I told the reporter on camera was exactly what I do every trip: I'm in Tokyo for a few days, so I send the suitcase I won't need right away ahead to my hotel in Nagoya. 

It's the first thing I do every time I land. My large suitcase goes on to Nagoya and is already in my room when I arrive.

The efficiency and hospitality of service in Japan is unparalleled. This is one of my favorite examples of it.

And it's exactly the kind of thing you feel the moment you arrive in Japan. The omtenatshi (hospitality) and efficient travel.

Come experience that culture of excellence and customer service for yourself and learn together with me about the leadership mindset and organizational practices that make these types of business results happen - through people.

items.content:
There's a reason the Daruma Temple is my favorite temple in all of Japan. 🇯🇵 And one of the key experiences of my Japan Leadership Experience.

I fell in love with darumas over a decade ago when I was living in Japan, and the figure has become my "mascot" in many ways!

The daruma doll embodies the proverb: "fall down seven times, get up eight."

When you have a goal, you fill in the doll's left eye. 

It serves as a visual reminder of the path of learning toward success. And when you achieve your goal, you fill in the other eye!

People bring their darumas here when their goal is complete, to be burned at the end of the year, a ritual of persistence, reflection, and renewal.

On this most recent visit, I brought a participant's daruma back to the temple from a past Japan Leadership Experience, at his request, for his completed goal of finishing his master's degree! (Congrats again Glenn Wilson!)

We don't just visit the temple. We take part in a Zen meditation with the head priest and talk about what these traditions teach us about business and leadership.

This is what makes my Japan Leadership Experience more than a trip: culture, reflection, and connection, alongside a remarkable group of global leaders. 

Plus special insights, curated experiences, and personal connections that I've developed over eleven years of living and working in Japan.

"Not one of you is going to make a comment that shows how smart you are."

That's what Gary Peterson told his 10 directors and VPs before they visited teams at O.C. Tanner.

No correcting. No second-guessing. No challenging their thinking.

Just listen, smile, and appreciate: "Wow, you guys are amazing." 

Because they are.

Creating the conditions for others to succeed takes a shift in identity and a shift in behavior. 

Sometimes the most powerful thing a leader can do is get out of the way and let their people shine. 

Stepping back can be stepping up, so that others can step in.

This is how O.C. Tanner has become a recognized company of excellence by Shingo Institute, The Association for Manufacturing Excellence (AME), Lean Enterprise Institute and Tugboat Institute.

What shifts will you make to create the conditions for YOUR team's success and impact?

"Learning to Lead, Leading to Learn" was released into the world 6 years ago this week -- on July 14, 2020!

In the height of the pandemic, during lockdown, I wasn't sure if it was appropriate to release a book. There was so much challenge and sorrow going on in our world. 

But I decided that this book, filled with stories overcoming mistakes and failures, finding the good in people, and leading with a focus on people and learning was something that could serve us all in our challenging times. 

And it has. And continues to do so.

With over 12,000 English language copies sold, multiple awards including the Shingo Institute Publication Award, endorsements from executives like Larry Culp, CEO of GE Aerospace, and translations into eight languages, the book has had an enduring global impact. 

The greatest gift for both Isao Yoshino (now 82 years old!) and me is knowing the positive impact it has had on YOU. 

Thank you for your reviews, your posts here on LinkedIn, and your positive direct messages. And for carrying its lessons into your own practice and those of the people around you.

This is what a Chain of Learning is all about. How we can show up with an attitude towards learning and a fundamental respect for people. 

That is really the secret to positive leadership. Positive impact. Lasting success.

Hold prescious what it means to be human and create the conditions for others to grow, learn, and achieve more than we could alone.

Thank you!!! 

#LearningToLead #LeadingToLearn #ChainOfLearning
